pr_title: core/oomd: Use oom-kill ServiceResult for oomd
pr_body:
To notify user of kill events from systemd-oomd we now use
`SERVICE_FAILURE_OOM_KILL` as the failure result.

`unit_check_oomd_kill` now calls `notify_cgroup_oom` to
update the service result to `oom-kill`.

We add a new xattr `user.oomd_ooms` to keep track of the OOM kills
initiated by systemd-oomd, this helps us resolve a race between sending
SIGKILL to processes and checking for OOM kill status from the xattr.

Related to: #20649
pr_comments:
Cool, this really looks pretty simple! I think in general we can also just enable it together with `ExitType=croup`, I don't see why that should be an issue.

Note that we *do* have the race condition currently that @Werkov was pointing out already. I think we can resolve this by changing the OOMD code though. i.e. looking at `oomd_cgroup_kill` we just need to move the `increment_oomd_xattr` to happen before the `cg_kill`/`cg_kill_recursive` call.

So, I think we can just add a patch to make that change, and then it should work. And, then maybe also enable the exit code for `ExitType=cgroup`.

CC: @anitazha

Hrm, except that we cannot export the number of processes that were killed into `user.oomd_kill` then.

So, we either need to change the definition of that attribute/counter, or we need another attribute to resolve the race condition.

> Hrm, except that we cannot export the number of processes that were killed into `user.oomd_kill` then.
> 
> So, we either need to change the definition of that attribute/counter, or we need another attribute to resolve the race condition.

The original oomd had 2 attributes: oomd_ooms which is incremented before SIGKILL and oomd_kill (the one systemd-oomd also has) which is incremented after. I didn't end up using oomd_ooms in the first iteration of systemd-oomd so I excluded it, but we can add it back to help mitigate a race in this case.

> @benzea do you think this is enough info to close https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/20649 ?

In my view, this is enough from the systemd side (We do need `ExitType=cgroup` for KDE at least). If we have this, we can simply write a desktop service that listens for all property changes on units (matching for `arg0` to be `org.freedesktop.systemd1.Unit` and listening for all `org.freedesktop.DBus.Properties.PropertiesChanged` signals otherwise).

looks pretty good. Though I am not sure it's a good idea to distinguish the two kinds of oom kills in the API. It appears to me that that's an implementaiton detail we should log about but not expose in the API otherwise, it doesn#t really matter if the kernel did this or us I'd argue.

Need help testing if the newly added xattr is working properly.

I'm having some issues testing due to the new systemd-oomd.socket changes added to v250, i've tried `sudo mkosi boot`(my guess is this just waits for a signal from the host system and therefore doesn't work when I disable systemd-oomd on my F35 v249 host) and `sudo mkosi qemu` (this just ends up performing a kernel OOM kill instead of using systemd-oomd[I have ManagedOOMMemoryPressure=kill set along with other configuration])

Hmm, we already have the subtree problem for kernel OOM kills, so it is not really anything new in that regard.

Maybe another idea could be to just only consider OOM kills on the leaf-node that contains the main service PID? That would basically delegate other leaf-nodes to the service, while we keep managing the main "service" cgroup from systemd.

> Maybe another idea could be to just only consider OOM kills on the leaf-node that contains the main service PID? That would basically delegate other leaf-nodes to the service, while we keep managing the main "service" cgroup from systemd.

I'm not sure I understand why we only focus on the main service PID. Wouldn't we want to go through this flow if a control command triggered the OOM kill as well?

can't to reply to the original comment for this one:
> added, although didn't we use oomd_ooms to help with the race condition where user.oomd_kill xattr might not have been updated by the time we reach here?

`oomd_kill` is only used as information here and not to deal with the race condition. Hence why if `oomd_kill` is unset or 0 the generic message is printed. There is a slight chance that we print the wrong number of processes if systemd-oomd is on its second attempt to kill a cgroup and `oomd_kill` isn't updated yet. But in practice the chance is low.

issue_context.title: systemd-oomd: Provide user feedback when killing a cgroup in a user slice
issue_context.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

Currently, systemd-oomd kills user programs without providing any further feedback to the user. This often leaves users confused as to why their program was suddenly terminated.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Ideally, users would receive a clear notification that systemd-oomd has killed (or is about to kill) one of their programs.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

/

**The systemd version you checked that didn't have the feature you are asking for**

v249

After some discussion with Lennart, we figured this could work by having systemd-oomd provide a D-Bus interface that allows clients to subscribe for oomd notifications. When oomd kills a program, it would then notify all subscribers via a D-Bus signal. Gnome/KDE could then subscribe to these notifications on the system bus and proxy them to the org.freedesktop.Notifications interface on the user bus.

cc @benzea
comments: Stupid question. But couldn't systemd itself rather than systemd-oomd export the information that the unit got into the failed state due to OOM?

> Stupid question. But couldn't systemd itself rather than systemd-oomd export the information that the unit got into the failed state due to OOM?

I'm pretty sure it could, but I figure oomd has more information available on why it's killing things that might be interesting to include in the D-Bus signals that systemd itself won't have. Either way, you'd need to proxy notifications the system bus (coming from either systemd or systemd-oomd) to the user bus.

I am not sure we should replicate the full oom meta info in pid 1, i.e. i think it's semantically nice this is separated. Yes, PID 1 should receive state changes from oomd, and track that, but detailed reports on what happened should not be proxied/replicated in PID1. I mean, doing such a game of proxying things along oh so many paths is something one should think twice about, and for every single step have a really good reason. But I am not convinced that a client preferring to talk to PID1 rather than oomd is a really good reason. Whether you talk to dbus service foo or dbus service bar really shouldn't matter, should it?

BTW, I'd like to extend the discussion to coredumps. Does GNOME currently have a story there? i.e. what happens if an app coredumps? is this handled by GNOME in any way? Or does the app just silently die? What about crashes in system services?

What does GNOME actually want there? Dumping super technical crash reports on users is probably a bad idea, but silently letting stuff crash, in particular stuff the user actually is working with sounds like a bad idea too. Some form of feedback is probably wise? 

I'd consider an OOM event oomd processed the same thing as a coredump when it comes to UI: something went wrong and I think the user deserves some form of explanatin why their app suddenly disappeared.
Also see https://pagure.io/fedora-workstation/issue/202 for previous discussion around this.

> BTW, I'd like to extend the discussion to coredumps. Does GNOME currently have a story there? i.e. what happens if an app coredumps? is this handled by GNOME in any way? Or does the app just silently die? What about crashes in system services?

GNOME has no handler for crashes. Ubuntu and Fedora have their own downstream crash handlers. Ubuntu's (apport) is incompatible with systemd-coredump afaik. Fedora's (ABRT) is integrated pretty well and gets its crash dumps from systemd.

> What does GNOME actually want there? Dumping super technical crash reports on users is probably a bad idea, but silently letting stuff crash, in particular stuff the user actually is working with sounds like a bad idea too. Some form of feedback is probably wise?

Ideally we would have our own version of ABRT in GNOME, but nobody wants to work on it, so I think status quo is fine for now.

OK, so, I believe that all want here is that the user is notified if a *user* process was killed by the OOM killer (either systemd-oomd or kernel). The systemd user instance already knows whether the process received an oomd kill and logs this information. If it just actually reported `oom-kill` as the service failure status string instead of `signal` then we would have enough information already.

i.e. just register for `PropertiesChanged` on `org.freedesktop.systemd1.Unit`; if we see `ActiveState` `failed` and `Result` being:
 * `oom-kill`: show OOM kill information
 * `core-dump`: prompt the user to start up the distribution-specific coredump handler

In both cases, we can try to extract the application ID from the systemd unit name and show e.g. the application icon to help the user identify the breaking process.

Now, there *is* a caveat for this, but I think that one is actually positive. i.e. when we kill an application managed sub-cgroup, then the unit will not go into a failed state, and we will not see it at all. This means, that browser tabs getting killed by systemd-oomd will not receive a notification or anything. I think this is actually an advantage, as the browsers will already have their own "oops, something went wrong" handler that allows the user to recover.


So, looking at systemd itself, we already have the `managed_oom_kill_last` information. Is there any reason to not expose this as `oom-kill` in the unit failure state? Right now the comment for the managed kills says:

```
                        /* This only logs for now. In the future when the interface for kills/notifications
                         * is more stable we can extend service results table similar to how kernel oom kills
                         * are managed. */
                        (void) unit_check_oomd_kill(u1);
```

Now, a fancy next step could be for mutter to actually listen to this information. It is starting to match windows to cgroups, so it can also match windows to systemd units now.

A bit more complicated, but when a systemd unit stops and a wayland client disappears unexpectedly, then mutter could try matching up the information. That way, one could potentially overlay the information about the process having been killed/dumping core on top of the last window state we have. Not trivial, but I think it should be possible to do.

Hey, coming back to this.

As we have `managed_oom_kill_last`, is there any reason to not expose this as `oom-kill` in the unit failure state?

Just few random ideas: it might be practical to have a distinct `oomd-kill` failure state (to ease troubleshooting). There is possible race of: cgroup emptiness notification, sigchld and xattr update, so things need to be sorted properly to get a stable and correct exit state. With the new `ExitType=cgroup` it's also more challenging to evaluate how it should translate into the exit state. (So in short, I don't see the reason but it should be done carefully.)

Actually I did make a comment here to eventually add a separate exit state for systemd-oomd kills, similar to the kernel one we have now: https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/a704137c20fcde3fa9077832d9ee29b89d6217e5/src/core/manager.c#L2633-L2636
It should be relatively simple to add as we can call into `notify_cgroup_oom()` the same way we do when processing a kernel OOM kill.

w.r.t the cgroup empty notification I think we can also add the `unit_check_oomd_kill()` in the cgroup empty flow to handle that case. But I hadn't been following when `ExitType=cgroup` was merged again so thanks for bringing that up Werkov. I can look into that.
@davidedmundson might want to provide some feedback here from the KDE side.

review_comments:
this also needs

```c
v = mfree(v);
```

to avoid leaking memory (since the pointer is reassigned in the `cg_get_xattr_malloc()` call below).
this should probably be a separate commit, no? and we should probably do unit_check_oom() here too, just in case.
